label: Snowflake
description: Tools to query and explore Snowflake with per-user, per-role access

tools.name: ListColumns
tools.description:
Get a table or view's columns, so you can select exact fields.

Load this before running a query, and select named columns rather than
everything. Works on views as well as tables. A not-found error usually
means the object is not granted to your role; re-check the table listing.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: The database the table lives in.

parameters.name: schema_name
parameters.description: The schema the table lives in.

parameters.name: table
parameters.description: The table or view to describe.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum columns to return (1-500). Defaults to 200.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting position. Defaults to 0.

output.description: The table's columns: name, type, nullability, comment

codeExample.tabLabel: Call the Tool with User Authorization

tools.name: ListDatabases
tools.description:
List the databases your role can access, newest-created first.

Snowflake returns only databases your current role is granted, so this is
already a per-user answer. Take a `name` and use it to list that database's
schemas. Use `name_pattern` to filter server-side rather than paging the
whole list.

parameters.name: name_pattern
parameters.description: Only include databases whose names match this case-insensitive SQL LIKE pattern, for example SALES% or %_RAW. Defaults to empty, which returns all of them.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum databases to return (1-200). Defaults to 50.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting position. Defaults to 0.

output.description: Databases the caller's role can access

codeExample.tabLabel: Call the Tool with User Authorization

tools.name: ListSchemas
tools.description:
List the schemas in a database that your role can access.

List the databases first to get a valid `database`. Then take a schema
`name` and list that schema's tables.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: The database to list schemas in.

parameters.name: name_pattern
parameters.description: Only include schemas whose names match this case-insensitive SQL LIKE pattern, for example PUBLIC or %_STAGING. Defaults to empty, which returns all of them.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum schemas to return (1-200). Defaults to 50.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting position. Defaults to 0.

output.description: Schemas in the database the caller's role can access

codeExample.tabLabel: Call the Tool with User Authorization

tools.name: ListTables
tools.description:
List the tables and views in a schema that your role can query.

List the schemas first to get a valid `database` and `schema_name`, then
load a table's columns before querying it.

Each row's `kind` is TABLE, VIEW, MATERIALIZED VIEW, or SEMANTIC VIEW. A
SEMANTIC VIEW cannot be read with an ordinary SELECT: it needs Snowflake's
SEMANTIC_VIEW(...) syntax, which this toolkit does not support, so skip
those when choosing something to query.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: The database the schema lives in.

parameters.name: schema_name
parameters.description: The schema to list tables and views in.

parameters.name: name_pattern
parameters.description: Only include tables and views whose names match this case-insensitive SQL LIKE pattern, for example ORDER% or %_FACT. Defaults to empty, which returns all of them.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum objects to return (1-200). Defaults to 50.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting position. Defaults to 0.

output.description: Tables and views in the schema the caller's role can access

codeExample.tabLabel: Call the Tool with User Authorization

tools.name: ListWarehouses
tools.description:
List the warehouses your role can run queries on.

An account usually has several, and Snowflake returns only the ones your
current role is granted, so this is already a per-user answer.

You only need this when a query has no warehouse to run on, either because
you have no default or because you want a different one. `size` is the cost
signal: prefer the smallest warehouse that fits the query. A SUSPENDED
warehouse is still usable, since Snowflake resumes it on use by default.

parameters.name: name_pattern
parameters.description: Only include warehouses whose names match this case-insensitive SQL LIKE pattern, for example ANALYTICS% or %_WH. Defaults to empty, which returns all of them.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum warehouses to return (1-200). Defaults to 50.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting position. Defaults to 0.

output.description: Warehouses the caller's role can use

codeExample.tabLabel: Call the Tool with User Authorization

tools.name: QueryRows
tools.description:
Run a read-only SELECT query and return the rows.

Only SELECT is allowed. Writes, DDL, role changes, and data movement are
rejected before the query reaches Snowflake, so this tool cannot modify
anything even if your Snowflake role would permit it.

The query runs under your own Snowflake identity, so your role and
Snowflake's row-access and masking policies decide what you can read. Two
users running identical SQL can legitimately get different results.

Load the table's columns before calling this, and name the columns you want
rather than selecting everything. `rows` is positional and
aligned to `columns`. `truncated` is true when more rows were available than
were returned.

Do not put LIMIT, OFFSET, or SQL comments in any clause; use the `limit` and
`offset` parameters, which are applied for you.

parameters.name: select_clause
parameters.description: The comma-separated columns to return, without the SELECT keyword.

parameters.name: from_clause
parameters.description: The table to read, without the FROM keyword. Fully qualify it as database.schema.table, or quote it as "DB"."SCHEMA"."TABLE".

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum rows to return (1-1000). Defaults to 100.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: 0-indexed starting row. Defaults to 0.

parameters.name: join_clause
parameters.description: A join. Omit the JOIN keyword for an inner join, for example orders o ON o.id = c.order_id. Include it for any other type, for example LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.id = c.order_id. Chain additional joins inside this one value. Defaults to empty, meaning no join.

parameters.name: where_clause
parameters.description: A filter, without the WHERE keyword. Defaults to empty, meaning no filter.

parameters.name: group_by_clause
parameters.description: Grouping columns, without the GROUP BY keyword. Defaults to empty.

parameters.name: having_clause
parameters.description: A post-aggregation filter, without the HAVING keyword. Defaults to empty.

parameters.name: qualify_clause
parameters.description: A filter over window-function results, without the QUALIFY keyword, for example ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1. Defaults to empty.

parameters.name: order_by_clause
parameters.description: Sort columns, without the ORDER BY keyword. Always sort when paging, otherwise row order is not stable between calls. Defaults to empty.

parameters.name: with_clause
parameters.description: One or more CTEs, without the WITH keyword, for example recent AS (SELECT ...). Defaults to empty.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: Session database so unqualified names resolve. Defaults to empty, meaning your own default database.

parameters.name: schema_name
parameters.description: Session schema so unqualified names resolve. Defaults to empty, meaning your own default schema.

parameters.name: warehouse
parameters.description: Warehouse to run on. Defaults to empty, meaning your own default warehouse.

join_clause.value: LEFT JOIN SALES_DB.PUBLIC.CUSTOMERS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id

tools.name: WhoAmI
tools.description:
Return the Snowflake identity every other tool uses, and the warehouse.

The role is the important field. It is what decides which objects the other
tools can see and which rows and cells come back, so two people calling the
same tool with the same arguments can legitimately get different data.

Pass `current_warehouse` straight through as the warehouse argument when
running a query. If it comes back empty this user has no default warehouse,
and a query must name one. The warehouse discovery tool lists the ones this
role may use, cheapest first by `size`.

This is the only place identity is reported. It runs no caller-supplied SQL,
so what it returns is always the identity the other tools will run under.

output.description: The Snowflake identity in effect, and the current warehouse

summary:
Arcade's Snowflake toolkit enables agents to query and explore Snowflake data warehouses with per-user, per-role access — every operation runs under the authenticated user's own Snowflake identity, so role assignments, row-access policies, and column masking apply automatically.

## Capabilities

- **Schema discovery** — enumerate accessible databases, schemas, tables/views (including materialized and semantic views), and individual columns; results are automatically scoped to the caller's role.
- **Warehouse discovery** — list warehouses the caller's role may use, with size metadata to help select the least expensive option for a given query.
- **Read-only SQL execution** — run `SELECT` statements with parameterized `limit`/`offset`; writes, DDL, role changes, and data-movement statements are rejected client-side before reaching Snowflake.
- **Identity inspection** — retrieve the active Snowflake username, role, and default warehouse so callers can reason about which objects and rows will be visible before issuing queries.
- **Per-user data isolation** — identical queries from different users can return different rows or masked column values based on each user's Snowflake grants and policies.

## OAuth

This toolkit authenticates via **OAuth 2.0** through Snowflake as the identity provider. Each user authorizes independently, and all tool calls execute under that user's Snowflake role.

## Secrets

- **`SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT_SUBDOMAIN`** — The account identifier subdomain for your Snowflake instance. This is the prefix used in your Snowflake login URL: for example, if your login URL is `https://xy12345.snowflakecomputing.com`, the value is `xy12345`. For accounts in non-default regions or on non-AWS clouds, the subdomain may include organization and account name segments (e.g., `myorg-myaccount`). Find this in the Snowflake console under **Admin → Accounts**, or refer to [Snowflake's account identifier documentation](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/admin-account-identifier) for the exact format your deployment uses.

Configure secrets in the Arcade dashboard or via the API: https://docs.arcade.dev/en/guides/create-tools/tool-basics/create-tool-secrets (secrets can also be managed at https://api.arcade.dev/dashboard/auth/secrets).
